5153559114d855c8e675.text: Both  DIRECT  and  REPORTED  SPEECH  give  information or  repeat a statement  that another  person said.  Both also use a  REPORTING  VERB  such as  said, told, asked,  etc.  DIRECT SPEECH Direct Speech repeats exactly  what someone said or quotes  the same words spoken.   Examples:  1. Lizel said, “I like your       story book.”  2. Hannah said, “I learned to       skate last week.”  REPORTED SPEECH Reported Speech (Indirect  Speech) is narrating or  retelling what the speaker  said in the past and so  there are changes in the  actual words.   Examples:  1. Lizel said that she liked       my story book.  2. Hannah said that she       had learned to skate the       week before.

6dbe1c79a36aee8fdab5.text: How are direct speech and reported speech different? There are 5 differences between the two and they are the following:

caa9c88582d66368788f.text: 1. Direct speech has quotation marks; reported speech does not use quotation marks. 2. In reported speech, the pronoun often changes. For example, in the above sentence no.1 with direct speech, the pronoun I is used, whereas the sentence with reported speech uses the pronoun she. 3. In reported speech, the word “that” is often used after said, but “that” is optional. In informal English we can leave “that” out especially after reporting verbs “say” and “tell.”

68e7b18ffac290a1136c.text: Examples: Mary says (that) her hair is soft.

b26100c871441ee897ab.text: He tells me (that) he cares for me. 4. In reported speech, the time words being used may also change if the report will be given at a different time. For example, the time words “last week” in the direct speech changes to “the week before” in the reported speech. Some common time words being used are the following:

53aaa47c7e606a77ca94.text: DIRECT  REPORTED SPEECH  DIRECT  REPORTED SPEECH  SPEECH    SPEECH    now  then, at that time  last night  the night before  today  that day, yesterday  this week  that week, last week  tonight  that night, last night  last month  the month before  yesterday  the day before  tomorrow  the next day

0331b1c2528654d80de6.text: 5. The verb in reported speech changes in tense.

7a97d44e973e9970a2eb.text: Let’s look at more examples for you to clearly see these differences and the rules in changing a direct speech to reported speech.

rows: Simple Present Karen said, “I bake cupcakes every day.”
Simple Past Karen said that she baked cupcakes every day.
The verb in the quoted speech changes from present tense to past tense.
Simple Past Karen said, “I baked cupcakes.”
Past Perfect Karen said that she had baked cupcakes.
The past perfect tense uses had +past participle form of the verb.
Present Perfect Karen said, “I have baked cupcakes.”
Past Perfect Karen said that she had baked cupcakes.
The past perfect tense uses had +past participle form of the verb.
Past Perfect Karen said, “I had baked cupcakes before Emman arrived.”
Past Perfect Karen said that she had baked cupcakes before Emman had arrived.”
If the verb in the direct speech is in the past perfect tense, there is no change in tense in the reported speech.
8f62180b33d4b48f00ae.text: DIRECT SPEECH REPORTED SPEECH REMARKS Simple Present Karen said, “I bake cupcakes every day.” Simple Past Karen said that she baked cupcakes every day. The verb in the quoted speech changes from present tense to past tense. Simple Past Karen said, “I baked cupcakes.” Past Perfect Karen said that she had baked cupcakes. The past perfect tense uses had +past participle form of the verb. Present Perfect Karen said, “I have baked cupcakes.” Past Perfect Karen said that she had baked cupcakes. The past perfect tense uses had +past participle form of the verb. Past Perfect Karen said, “I had baked cupcakes before Emman arrived.” Past Perfect Karen said that she had baked cupcakes before Emman had arrived.” If the verb in the direct speech is in the past perfect tense, there is no change in tense in the reported speech.

labels.text: Now that you have learned how to create direct and reported speech statements, let
us look at how these statements can be used in a longer discourse or different
genres. Read and examine the sample short story and comic strip below.
Reported Speech is usually introduced by a verb in the past tense but it can also be
introduced by a verb in  present tense:
This is usual when we are:
a. reporting a conversation that is still going on
b. reading a letter and reporting what it says
c. reading instructions and reporting them
reporting a statement that someone makes very often, e.g.
When the reporting verb is in a present, present perfect or future tense, we can
report the direct speech without any change of tense:
Paul (phoning from the station): I’m trying to get a taxi.
Ann (to Mary, who is standing beside her): Paul says he is trying to get a taxi.
. Direct Speech can sometimes have inverted reporting verb and subject. This can be
done with most of the reporting verbs except “tell”. This usually happens in literature
such as in stories and novels.
“I washed the dishes already,” Anton said.
“Paul got a perfect score,” the teacher announced.
Source: Eastwood, John. 2002. Oxford Guide To English Grammar.
